passage: On festival morning at the preschool, the children lined up to light a clay lamp. Farhan, the teacher, showed the steps, but Seema already knew them from home. “Right hand first,” she told the boy behind her. “Then we fold our hands and say thank you.” She lit hers carefully, tongue poking out with the effort. The boy copied her, and so did three others. One girl stood at the back, unsure, hands tucked into her sleeves. Seema tugged her forward. “Stand here, I'll show you.” Farhan smiled. Seema whispered to herself, “I did it right.”

qa.q: Which hand did Seema say to use first?
qa.a: Seema said to use the right hand first.

qa.q: How does Seema feel when she whispers, “I did it right”?
qa.a: Seema feels proud and happy, and seems glad to be doing what her family does.

qa.q: What did Seema do that helped the girl at the back?
qa.a: Seema pulled the unsure girl forward and offered to show her the steps, so the girl could take part.

qa.q: What might the girl at the back have been feeling with her hands in her sleeves?
qa.a: The girl was probably shy or worried about doing it wrong, since she did not know the steps yet.

grounding: A child joins in festival lights at school and delights in doing the steps right, which makes her feel like one of us.

passage: I'm Nandini, and I live next door to Bidisha. I was at her fifth birthday. Before the cake, her grandfather sat in his chair, and Bidisha bent to touch his feet. “Aashirwad,” she announced, though she said it as “ashi-wat,” and he tapped her head, chuckling. She ran to fetch a plate of sweets for the old aunt. Then she stood on tiptoe by the cake, eyes squeezed shut, for the family's little wish. I can't know what she felt inside. But afterwards she looked around at every face, as if to check she'd done it right.

qa.q: What did Bidisha do before the cake in front of her grandfather?
qa.a: Bidisha bent to touch his feet.

qa.q: Why might Bidisha have looked at every face after the wish?
qa.a: Bidisha seems to care whether she did the family's custom right, and wants to see that people are pleased and that she belongs.

qa.q: How could a relative respond to Bidisha's checking looks?
qa.a: A relative could smile and say, “You did it just like us,” so that Bidisha's pride in belonging is confirmed.

qa.q: How might Bidisha's grandfather see her mispronounced “ashi-wat”?
qa.a: Bidisha's grandfather seems touched and amused, since he tapped her head and chuckled instead of correcting her.

grounding: A child joins in birthday customs and delights in doing them right, seen by someone next door.

passage: On Lucia morning in Uppsala, Jin woke before it was light. Mormor Ulla helped him into a long white shirt and gave him a paper star on a stick. Mamma, Pappa and his cousins lined up in the dark hallway. Jin held his star very straight and walked slowly, singing the only words he knew, 'Sankta Lucia', loud and proud. When they reached Morfar's room with the saffron buns, Morfar clapped. Jin whispered to Mormor, 'Did I do it right?' She nodded, and he beamed.

qa.q: What did Mormor Ulla give Jin to hold?
qa.a: A paper star on a stick.

qa.q: What does Jin asking 'Did I do it right?' show?
qa.a: He wanted very much to do the custom properly and felt proud and delighted to be part of it.

qa.q: How did the family help Jin join the tradition?
qa.a: Mormor dressed him, gave him a star and a place in the line, and nodded when he asked, so he felt he belonged.

qa.q: How might Morfar feel watching Jin in the procession?
qa.a: Likely happy and touched to see his grandson join the family's Lucia morning.

grounding: A young child joins a family festival custom and delights in doing it right.

passage: At the playschool's Diwali morning, Pallavi ma'am showed the children how to light a diya: hold it steady, let the teacher bring the matchstick, keep fingers away from the flame. Eshaan held his clay diya with both hands like a baby bird. 'Like Dadi does it!' he said. When the flame caught, he gasped and looked at his friends. Mehul and Anu had theirs lit too. Eshaan carefully placed his in the row on the rangoli and folded his hands, eyes shut tight, just like at home.

qa.q: Who brought the matchstick to light the diyas?
qa.a: The teacher, Pallavi ma'am.

qa.q: What does Eshaan saying 'Like Dadi does it!' suggest?
qa.a: He felt excited and proud, happy to be doing the custom the way his family does.

qa.q: How did Pallavi ma'am make the custom safe and joyful?
qa.a: She showed each step clearly, lit the diyas herself, and let the children place them and pray in their own way.

qa.q: What might Mehul and Anu feel with their own diyas lit beside Eshaan's?
qa.a: They probably shared the excitement, so the row of lights felt like something the whole group did together.

grounding: A young child joins a festival custom at school and delights in doing it the way the family does.

passage: Saturday: Bidisha watched Pallavi pishi draw alpana on the floor with rice paste, swirling tiny feet all the way from the door. 'Lakshmi's footsteps,' pishi said. Bidisha tried one and made a blob. She frowned. Sunday: she practised on the balcony with chalk, tongue poking out, making little feet over and over. Tuesday, puja day: pishi handed her the bowl. Bidisha drew three wobbly feet near the door, all by herself. Thamma smiled and said, 'Now Lakshmi will come to our house.' Bidisha stood in the doorway all evening, guarding her footprints.

qa.q: What did Pallavi pishi draw with rice paste?
qa.a: Alpana, with tiny feet from the door: Lakshmi's footsteps.

qa.q: How did Bidisha feel on puja day after drawing the feet?
qa.a: She felt proud and happy, guarding her footprints all evening after Thamma's words.

qa.q: What helped Bidisha learn the custom?
qa.a: Watching pishi, practising with chalk on her own, and then being trusted with the bowl on puja day.

qa.q: How might Pallavi pishi feel seeing Bidisha's wobbly feet?
qa.a: She would likely feel pleased and warm, seeing the tradition passed on to the next child.

grounding: Over several days a young child learns a family festival custom and delights in doing it right.

passage: The power went out just as the family gathered to set up the Christmas crib. Grandma lit candles. Five-year-old Maria held the tiny baby figure very carefully in both hands. "Not yet," whispered her cousin Jahnavi. "Baby comes at midnight." Maria nodded seriously and waited, clutching it. When everyone sang a carol in the dark, she sang the words she knew, loudly, and hummed the rest. At midnight Grandma said, "Now, Maria." She laid the baby in the straw, then looked round at everyone. "I did it right!" Uncle clapped, and Maria clapped too.

qa.q: Who lit the candles when the power went out?
qa.a: Grandma lit candles.

qa.q: How can you tell Maria wanted to do the custom properly?
qa.a: She waited seriously, clutching the figure until midnight, and announced "I did it right!", which shows she felt proud and grown-up.

qa.q: How did Jahnavi help Maria join in?
qa.a: Jahnavi whispered the family rule, that the baby comes at midnight, so Maria knew what to do.

qa.q: What might Grandma feel when Maria lays the baby in the straw?
qa.a: She is likely happy and touched to see the youngest carrying on the family's Christmas custom.

grounding: Shows a young child joining a family Christmas custom and delighting in doing it right, which makes her feel one of the family.
